title: Async span multiplexing and histogram bucketing to cut observability overhead
creator: Marin Vega
description:
Summary: Reduce CPU and p99 tail latency pressure from our observability pipeline by (1) introducing an asynchronous span multiplexing layer that coalesces short-lived internal spans into aggregated trace envelopes and (2) moving histogram metrics to fixed bucketing with server-side normalization. Goal: lower runtime CPU and memory footprint from telemetry, reduce per-request tracing overhead, and cut exported span/metric cardinality without losing signal for alerting and debugging.

Why now: Recent load tests show telemetry processing contributes up to 18% CPU at peak for small inference slices and increases tail latency for short RPCs. Previous attempts focused on sampling and exporter batching, but we still have high in-process costs from synchronous span creation and high-cardinality histogram labels. This ticket is a targeted tech-debt cleanup to deploy low-risk behavioral changes with measurable economics.

What we'll change: 
- Add an asynchronous span multiplexer inside the runtime tracing hook that buffers short-lived spans (<5ms) and emits aggregated envelopes periodically (configurable window). The multiplexer preserves essential attributes (span count, error flags, latency quantiles) while dropping rarely used free-form tags.
- Replace dynamic histogram buckets with a standardized fixed-bucket schema for high-frequency metrics (seq-length, token-latency, batch-size) and perform normalization on the exporter to shrink payload size.
- Switch the current synchronous log/trace writer to a background worker pool with backpressure-aware queues and bounded memory caps. Provide an escape hatch to bypass multiplexing for debug builds.
- Upgrade opentelemetry-go to the latest stable that supports non-blocking exporters and the streaming metric SDK. Update otel instrumentation hooks accordingly.
- Add feature flags and config knobs to toggle multiplexing, histogram mode, and buffer sizes at runtime via the Console.

Success metrics (measured in canary region): 
- CPU usage attributable to telemetry code reduced by >=12% during 95th-percentile load windows.
- Per-request median latency impact from tracing reduced to <1ms (was 3–4ms).
- Exported span count reduced by >=40% for high-throughput endpoints without loss of alerting signal.
- Metric cardinality for token-latency histogram reduced by >=60% (fewer unique bucket labels).

Non-goals / constraints: 
- We will not change business-critical sampling policies or remove customer-facing trace ids. 
- This ticket avoids schema changes visible to customers; exporter-side normalization is internal and compatible with existing dashboards.

Rollout plan: 
1) Unit + integration tests + perf harness locally.
2) Merge behind feature flag. Canary deploy to region us-west-2 with 5% traffic for a 48h window. Monitor cpu/latency, error rates, logs, and alert fidelity.
3) Expand to 25% then full rollout, each stage with a minimum 24h hold and automated rollback triggers (error rate > 2x baseline OR cpu increase >10%).

Rollback plan: If p99 latency or errors increase during canary, flip feature flag off and revert exporter config. If memory pressure increases, decrease multiplex window and buffer sizes.

Testing & validation: 
- End-to-end perf harness against production trace load (daily).
- Compare exported span/metric counts and dashboard regressions.
- QA runbook to validate debug span emission and trace continuity.

Notes: This work is intended to be complementary to prior tracing optimization tickets but uses a different approach (aggregation instead of aggressive sampling). We expect to follow up with archive/long-term storage optimizations if this reduces export load as expected.
acceptance_criteria: Telemetry CPU attribution down by >=12% in canary compared to baseline
Median tracing overhead per request < 1ms in canary
Exported span count reduced by >=40% for targeted endpoints
No alert/regression on core error budgets during canary period
